I love this little memo because it illustrates perfectly a number of points I've been making about the nature of for-profit business motivations and how they affect what happens.

Granted, occasionally one sees naive people try to make things better. These people almost always fail. We can and do improve performance for specific scenarios that people with the ability to allocate resources believe impact business goals, but this work is Sisyphean. There's no formal or informal program of systemic performance improvement. We started caring about security because pre-SP3 Windows XP was an existential threat to the business. Our low performance is not an existential threat to the business.

Here we see something interesting. When for-profit motivation is dominant, then the quality of the product and service must never exceed a minimum necessary to make the sale. Thus the product is destined to be right around the mediocre level. It's destined to be acceptable, or the customer wouldn't buy it. But it's never going to be excellent, because excellence for its own sake is extremely wasteful from a business POV, especially if you know that the last 20% of work requires the 80% of effort, whereas 80% of something can be accomplished with the 20% of effort. It's the ole 80/20 principle, and/or the law of diminishing returns. Excellence is expensive and for-profit motivation conflicts with the notion of excellence for its own sake.

Second point:

See, component owners are generally openly hostile to outside patches: if you're a dev, accepting an outside patch makes your lead angry (due to the need to maintain this patch and to justify in in shiproom the unplanned design change), makes test angry (because test is on the hook for making sure the change doesn't break anything, and you just made work for them), and PM is angry (due to the schedule implications of code churn). There's just no incentive to accept changes from outside your own team. You can always find a reason to say "no", and you have very little incentive to say "yes".

And here we see something that makes Karl Marx nod his head: disenfranchisement. Fact: you don't own what you're working on. You're just being paid a flat wage. Why should you pour your heart into something that isn't for primarily your own benefit but is primarily for the benefit of your employer? Most workers know this if not consciously then subconsciously and will strive to do minimum acceptable amount of work. So they'll work well enough to avoid being fired, and that's it. There is no incentive for excellence beyond that because the product isn't yours and the primary benefit isn't yours. Once you do what you need to do to collect your paycheck, you're not able to work for yourself anymore. Everything above and beyond the minimum you need to do to keep your job and collect your wage in a for-profit environment is for the sake of the employer. Of course even the minimal things you do are also primarily for the sake of the employer, but this isn't obvious. This requires analysis to understand. Whereas it is blatantly obvious on its face that once you're done doing enough work to avoid being fired, there is no longer any incentive to bend your back. The product isn't yours. You don't own your own labor or the products of your labor. You are intellectually and emotionally separated from what you're doing at work. That's disenfranchisement.
